newsitem.title: USA: Ill. electric dereg little impact - state official.
newsitem.headline: Ill. electric dereg little impact - state official.

text.p: Illinois Commerce Commission Chairman Dan Miller said Thursday a massive state electric deregulation bill up for consideration in the fall would foreclose competition and have little impact on rates.
But while the bill has "major problems," commission members believe it can be fixed and a progressive plan adopted by lawmakers, Miller said in an interview Thursday.

"If the utilities continue to retain their virtual exclusive franchise -- and in this case it would be an exclusive franchise territory -- and be allowed pricing flexibility of the kind envisioned in this bill, at the end of 10 years Illinois would end up with rates that are still above the midwest average and I cannot see how competition would even begin to emerge under the terms of this bill," Miller said.
The proposal passed the Illinois House in the waning days of the General Assembly's session in May, but senators opted to consider the plan in the fall veto session.

Senate President James "Pate" Philip has asked the commerce commission to provide input on the bill. The members discussed the bill Wednesday and plan a written response in late July or early August, Miller said.
"No commissioner, including myself is trying to torpedo the bill as it stands," Miller said. "It just needs work. It can be fixed and it can result in a progressive piece of legislation."
The legislation provides residential rate cuts of from 5 percent to 15 percent beginning in 1998 and phased in residential customer choice of utility beginning in 2000.
All commercial/industrial customers would be given choice of utility by 2000 with large industrial customers receiving the option beginning in October 1999.
The plan also included 50 percent recovery for investments made during the regulatory environment that may not be recoverable under competition, known in the industry as "stranded costs."

"The real problem is that there is no clear path to competition at the end of all of this trouble," Miller said. "The incumbent utilities can price under their own costs. They can waive certain fees and other charges that competitive suppliers cannot.

"It is a matter of favoring the incumbent utility to such an extent that no competitor is going to try to come to Illinois to try to sell electricity here in what is a very high cost market," Miller said.
Commonwealth Edison, a subsidiary of Unicom Corp, supports the plan and also projects it would cost the utility $1.6 billion in rate reductions over three years beginning in 1998.
Edison spokeswoman Marjorie Benzkofer called the plan competitive and the result of compromises on all sides. Most other states have allowed 100 percent recovery for stranded costs, she said.
"We think that it addresses more issues than any other proposal either passed or pending anywhere in the United States," Benzkofer said.
Central Illinois Light, a subsidiary of CILCORP, opposed the plan and in a statement Thursday said the bill does not provide enough economic benefits for consumers or clearly define stranded costs.
The lengthy transition period should be shortened and the charges assessed for the transition should be cut to encourage competition, Central Illinois Light contends.
All customers should be permitted choice at the same time or on a shortened schedule and the commerce commission should continue to have the authority to lower rates below bill mandates.

Bill supporters also include Illinois Power, a subsidiary of Illinova Corp; Central Illinois Public Service Corp; Citizens Utility Board; Illinois Retail Merchants Association; and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers.
